---
applyTo: "app/core/**/*.py,app/sep/deps.py,app/inventory/deps.py,app/tasks/deps.py,app/sep/apps/framework/**/*.py"
---

# Cross-Cutting Changes — Shared Helpers & Side Effects

Diffs to these paths fan out across all three sub-applications. The bug class this file targets is a change that **passes its own tests** but breaks a caller elsewhere because the new behaviour wasn't audited against every call site.

## Shared-helper changes — audit every caller

When a PR touches `app/core/**`, `app/<service>/deps.py`, `app/sep/apps/framework/**`, or a base class in `*/models.py` / `*/crud.py` whose subclasses live in multiple packages, the PR description should enumerate every call site and explain how the new behaviour preserves each caller's contract.

Specifically:

- **Signature changes** — every caller must be updated; per-caller justification when defaults or arg types change.
- **Emitted SQL changes** — when a DB helper changes its compiled SQL, callers using column types the new SQL doesn't handle fail at runtime, not compile time. Verify each caller's column types.
- **Return-shape changes** — adding/removing/reordering tuple elements, list → iterator, `None` → sentinel breaks every caller that destructures or matches the old shape.
- **Side-effect changes** — a helper that gained or lost an emit silently rewires every caller.
- **Exception-surface changes** — a helper that starts raising (or raises a new exception type) where it previously returned exposes every ungated caller to an uncaught failure path. This applies regardless of package (`app/tasks/**`, `app/inventory/**`, not only `app/core/**`). For each caller confirm it is gated by a `try/except` that persists a terminal state, a registered exception handler, or a short-circuit; a synchronous HTTP route with none of those turns the new raise into a bare 500 — a blocker.

When a surfaced caller only wraps or re-exports the result rather than consuming it, the audit is not done — recurse into the wrapper's callers. A one-level fan-out that stops at a wrapper (e.g. `get_executor_for_task` around `get_executor`) is blind to the actual consumers.

Flag any diff to these paths that lacks a caller audit. Canonical incident: a `func_json_extract` rewrite framed as a "no-op simplification" broke one caller whose column type the new form didn't support.

## Side-effect coverage on state-field writers

When a diff hooks a side-effect (`schedule_annotation`, `audit.log`, `metrics.emit`, `notify_*`, `alert_*`, `webhook.fire`) into a function that **observes** a state field — a polling loop, a `sync_*` method, an `on_change` handler — the diff is incomplete unless **every other writer to that state field in the same module** also routes through the side-effect.

Failure mode: hooking the side-effect into one observer and missing a parallel write site that mutates the field directly. The missing-behaviour bug doesn't show up in the diff scan — no added/changed line exists on the missing path.

To check:

1. Identify the **state field** the side-effect is keyed on (e.g. `queue_item.status`, `alert.acknowledged`).
2. Grep every writer (`<field> =`) in the affected file and sibling files in the same app/service.
3. For each match, ask: does this writer eventually trigger the side-effect? Writers that call the observer the new hook lives in inherit the side-effect. Writers that bypass it silently drop the side-effect — flag as **Critical**.
4. When the field has more than ~3 writers and the side-effect is hooked at only one observer, recommend moving the side-effect to the manager `save()` layer — that is the lowest common write site. Note a **mapper event does not cover the bulk paths**: `update_where()` / `delete_where()` emit a Core-level bulk statement and bypass the identity map, so `event.listen(Model, "after_update", …)` never fires for them.

**The enumeration must be closed.** Every writer either fires the side-effect or is named as excluded *with its reason*. A write-up that lists the covered paths and one reasoned carve-out, leaving other writers unmentioned, is **not** closed — and is worse than no enumeration at all, because a documented exclusion signals the writer set *was* considered, and that signal is what suppresses the grep. If you can name why one path is out of scope, you've already accepted the obligation to say where the boundary falls; state it for the whole set. The tell to look for in a PR description: one reasoned exclusion sitting beside an unmentioned one.

## Changing what a shared predicate or dispatch surface selects

Changing what a shared predicate or dispatch surface **selects** — by widening it, narrowing it, or gating it — changes behaviour at every existing call site. Both directions share the property that makes them dangerous: the reroute is invisible at the definition site, so the blast radius goes unexamined.

- *Widening* looks purely additive (nothing removed, no signature narrowed), which is exactly why it goes unchecked — but a value that used to fall through to a default now matches a specific handler.
- *Narrowing or gating* looks like a local tightening: one new condition on one predicate. But it silently **removes** inputs from every consumer's selected set, and the consumers that break are the ones asking a *different question* than the new condition answers. A predicate consulted for a structural question ("does this parent have leaves to render?") doesn't stop being consulted when it acquires an authorization question ("may you write this?") — it just starts answering the wrong one.

Before changing one in either direction, enumerate what **dispatches on** it: `except` sites (`git grep -nE "except (<Class1>|<Class2>)"`), `isinstance` checks, `exception_handler` registrations, and DI / routing tables (`dependency_overrides`, `task_routes`, `@register`). **Registry registrations are the easiest to miss**, because the coupling is by *type* and leaves no trace where the type is defined — a class in `app/core/exceptions.py` carries no hint that `app/sep/main.py` registers a dedicated handler for it, but one grep for `exception_handler` finds it.

The same audit applies to an enum, a response model, a DI alias, or a settings class — anywhere a consumer's behaviour is selected by matching against the surface you're changing. Two exemptions: a refactor whose truth table is unchanged (nothing re-selects, so no consumer moves), and module-local helpers that don't cross a module boundary — *shared* is the trigger, not call-site count.

## Correctness patterns on shared paths

- **A name the handler logs must be bound before the `try`.** An `except` block referencing a variable assigned *inside* its own `try` raises `NameError` whenever the failure happens before that assignment — and the `NameError` escapes the handler, so the very failure the block existed to absorb now propagates. Worst in a **swallow-all** handler whose whole contract is that it cannot fail (a best-effort recorder, a metrics hook, a notification send): the bug converts "this side-effect quietly did nothing" into "this side-effect broke the caller". Pre-bind to `None` before the `try` — logging `None` says the value was never read, which is exactly what happened. When adding an identifier to an existing failure log, check where it's bound relative to the handler before assuming the change is cosmetic.
- **Order guards by cost, not by narrative, on a hot path.** When a function is called on a polling or fan-out path and returns early most of the time, the review question isn't "is the no-op path correct?" but **"what does the no-op path cost?"** A cheap guard (a column already in memory, a flag on an object the caller holds) must run *before* an expensive one (a DB round-trip, an HTTP call, a file read) — otherwise the overwhelmingly common outcome is: pay the expensive thing, then discover there was nothing to do. The tell is a best-effort hook whose precondition is checked *inside* the function, after it has opened a session or issued a join, while both call sites hold an object carrying that precondition for free (sessions are built with `expire_on_commit=False`, so a status is often already free on the detached object). Gate at the call site where the cheap fact lives and keep the internal guard as defence-in-depth.
- **Accept every input the documented contract admits.** A parser or resolver must not reject or silently drop input its stated contract accepts. An accepted set *narrower* than the contract fails in the direction that leaves no trace: valid input is silently misread rather than refused, so there's no raise, no log, and nothing pointing at the boundary. The contract is whichever the helper claims — a published format spec (a Markdown fence matcher requiring the line to end right after the language token rejects a valid CommonMark info string, then reads that block's *closing* fence as an *opening* one and misclassifies everything after it) or its own docstring (an AST walk collecting only `ast.Name` targets, whose docstring promises "every module-level assignment-target name", misses `cache, warm = build()`). Widen the accepting construct to the contract or narrow the documented contract to what the code accepts — never leave the two disagreeing — then test the widened variants. Both shapes are typically *dormant*: the corpus in front of the author happened to use only the narrow form, which is why no failing test exists and why "it passes today" is not evidence the boundary is right.
- **A promise of totality must hold on every value the annotation admits.** When a docstring promises total, non-raising behaviour ("a missing `meta`, unparseable YAML, or an absent key all resolve to `None` rather than raising", "this method never raises"), every value the parameter annotation admits must reach a `return`, not a `raise`. The recurring tell: a type-narrowing ladder guarding every level it *indexes* and none of the ones it *passes onward* — a value checked only for truthiness before being handed to a parser is unguarded, since `yaml.safe_load` / `json.load` accept a stream-like or `str` and raise outside their documented error family on anything else. **Narrow the input you hand onward; do not widen the `except`** — ruff `BLE001` is project-wide, and a blanket `except Exception` converts a specific contract into a silent catch-all. A deliberate classified catch-all is legitimate where the promise genuinely is "never raises", but it must be explicit and `noqa`'d (`app/core/requests/remote_api.py::check_connectivity` is the sanctioned example).
- **Refusal posture must be consistent within a module.** A branch that **discards** input — `except ValueError: return None`, a `continue` on a malformed record, a filter dropping an unrecognised member — is a refusal, not a non-event. When any refusal path in a module logs, every sibling refusal path must too; a **mixed posture** is the tell, because the branches that do log are what make the silent ones look considered. The cost is diagnosability, not correctness: the silent path usually can't be reached by today's inputs, which is why no test covers it and why it survives review — it becomes reachable when an upstream contract drifts (a new enum member, a renamed key), and then the failure presents as absent output with nothing in the log pointing at the boundary that dropped it.
- **A redundant guard's eliminating branch may be an `except`, not only an `if`.** A guard standing immediately before a `try` whose handler already returns the same value for the same input is dead — `if marker is None: return None` above `try: return BackupType(marker) except ValueError: return None`. **Verify what the call actually raises on the guarded input; don't pattern-match the shape** — this is a carve-out, not a footnote, because the identical shape around a different callable is load-bearing and dropping the guard there converts a graceful `None` into an uncaught crash. `SomeEnum(None)` (no `_missing_` override) raises `ValueError`, so the guard is redundant; `int(None)` / `float(None)` / `UUID(None)` raise `TypeError`, so the guard is load-bearing. Check for a `_missing_` override before applying the enum row.
- **`ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` is live on hand-built models.** Direct `Model(field=...)` construction **does** validate — an unexpected kwarg raises `ValidationError`. Only `model_construct()` skips validation (extra data is silently ignored there even under `forbid`). Flag the config as dead only when *every* construction path is `model_construct()` and no untrusted input reaches the model.
- **A default is a claim about the shipped artifact, not about the repo.** Flipping a feature's default — or converting an opt-in to an opt-out — asserts that the new default's preconditions hold **wherever the software runs**, and the repo is not that place: it doesn't contain the published image, the operator's rendered config, or the tag they'll pull. Ship the precondition check together with the flip, verify it against a real artifact of each polarity, and fail with the remedies named. The failure is legible-versus-illegible, not present-versus-absent: without the check the precondition still fails, it just fails later, further from its cause, as a downstream step whose error names something else entirely.

## Dependency aliases live in `deps.py`

`Annotated[..., Depends(...)]` aliases MUST live in `app/<service>/deps.py` (or app `deps.py`), never in `routes.py`, `models.py`, or `loader.py`. When a dep helper exists (`get_pmm_api`, `get_or_create_alert_folder`), routes and tasks MUST use it — don't construct clients or do lookups inline.

## When to extract a dependency

A route handler should receive **prepared** objects via `Depends(...)` and do only HTTP-layer work. Extract when the body opens with a multi-step lookup / fetch / validation block. Extract feature-flag / config-gate guards (`if not <settings>.<FLAG>: raise HTTPForbiddenException(...)`) and inline resource-state preconditions (`if task.protected: raise HTTPConflictException(...)`) even at 2-3 lines — they belong in the route signature for OpenAPI visibility and reuse. Don't extract single attribute accesses, response construction, or endpoint-specific error formatting.

**Reuse first, extract second.** When the package's `deps.py` already exports a typed alias covering the same resolution, flag any inline invocation of the underlying function regardless of line count — the existing alias overrides the 1–2 line threshold. A sibling input-shape route (Form vs JSON, sync vs async) that needs the same prep chain gets a parallel typed alias, not inline code.

For each opening block in a new route handler, ask "could this object have arrived via `Depends`?" If yes and the block is more than 1–2 lines, flag. Guards are exempt from the line-count threshold.
